A Time of War : A Memoir Across Three Generations

Dear reader, it is with great excitement that I offer this expansive work for your consideration: A recently unearthed, voluminous manuscript – an epic memoir written over the course of three generations. It is a work as monumental and daunting as it is groundbreaking - a glimpse into the inner workings of the true scientific mind.

Upon discovery of these immaculate pages, I, suffering great personal expense, set forth to ensure the general publication and distribution of this important history. It is a work that will perhaps elucidate upon and justify the eccentric reputations of my forebears.

While I admit that I am biased in this appraisal, as it is my own exemplary lineage which is documented, I submit this comprehensive prosopography in as accurate a condition as I can muster. As one will soon attest, it is a chronicle of events of a decidedly fantastical nature, yet my research confirms it to be as true and vital a work as has ever been seen in print.

However, I must offer a word of caution to those with weaker constitutions. While these pages hold a brilliant catalogue of achievements, they also boldly depict the setbacks encountered along the journey. Gruesome, grim, and horrifying as they may be, I have included their spine-chilling contents as originally written. As one might expect, in exposing the base components of the universe, we uncover both light and darkness in equal measure. For without darkness, we cannot appreciate the brilliance of the light.
Taking Sides

My father was a genius! I state this now, not with the naïveté of my initial discovery of his journal, but as a time-tested statement of truth. It is why I pen these words today for posterity and to affirm with deep conviction what some may erroneously refer to as mad science.

When I first arrived at my father's manor, I carried the same skepticism any normal individual would. Weary as I was from the excursion across the Hungarian plains, the cold, gray walls of the villa with its oppressive iron gates chilled me to my marrow. When the disfigured caretaker — the only person privileged with the knowledge — revealed to me a false door and spiraling staircase that descended to a secret laboratory, the grim discovery did nothing to soothe my nerves. In fact, the sight of jars filled with preserved flesh and the astringent stench of chemicals aggravated my frail state, leaving me to take my suppers in the bedroom for several weeks.

But, it was this same dark discovery that eventually roused me from my illness. For as I pored over the journal bequeathed to me and surveyed page after page of formulaic experimentation, my apprehensions melted. I felt trepidacious, yet unreservedly enthusiastic at the ethical implications of this great task!

Yet even after the disquiet within my soul was relieved, the nearby village rattled my window panes with cacophonous revelry. At first, I kept my visits to the borough brief and infrequent. It seemed that whenever I turned my head I would lock eyes with a cautious observer, and I felt the entire town's steel gaze like daggers tickling the back of my skull. I could only speculate that my siblings endured the same sordid treatment.

It was my spouse, using my extended rest to become better acquainted with the village, who explained how spirited political discourse was the source of this commotion. Then I could discern the rally cry of their evening demonstrations as they spoke of disobedience, the end of monarchy, and civil war.

I began to realize the potential boon that war could provide for my research. If the people shared a mere fraction of the passion that now stoked the fires of my heart, how easily they would embrace my scientific assistance! While my father's ambitions were strong, his solitary existence had doomed his ideas to obscurity.

I would not repeat this error. I would brave the jeers of the populace to guide them in the art of warfare. My efforts would determine the course of this conflict. And when the time comes, it will be my science that will emerge from the flames of war as the true victor!
War on the Horizon

The spectre of war haunted the small village. This ideological tension would erupt in loud displays and gatherings of the peasantry near the Town Hall. For all the folderol, I began to cherish the moments when the eerie stillness of the evening was broken by anguished yells.

The Separatists felt alienated by the aristocratic government and wished to secede. Their brash tactics aimed to incite a democratic revolt among the proletariat. The Unified Monarchists feared the anarchic destabilization of the economy at such a key moment during industrialization. I was quickly able to determine that the town supported the {{0=...|Separatists|...}}.

Plagued by Conflict

If one can call the prospect of perpetual conflict stabilizing, my life settled into a somewhat steady routine. During the day, the sound of distant gunfire rumbled through the halls of my estate as silver plumes of smoke billowed beyond the mountainous horizon, casting tendril-like shadows across the land — a constant reminder of civil war. At night, the rare spectacle of an explosion brightening the sky surprised me with how viscerally I reacted.

Soldiers in their bright regalia keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost, waving the brilliant orange flag of royalty. The Monarchy had claimed victory from afar after stationing their ranks across the region, but as scuffles remained constant, this declaration was all pomp without substance. The Monarchy drafted citizens into their ranks and levied penalties against those who showed disloyalty.

The inference that one of my standing should owe a debt of servitude to those who already tax my earnings into oblivion was enough to make me spill my tea. And to what end, I wondered? Could peace be mustered in a populace kept so distant from the individuals who ruled it? It was called the industrial revolution for a reason, was it not?

But, I must admit, the safety that the Monarchy afforded appealed to my pocketbook. Appeasing the Monarchy would ensure money and influence, but it also appeared — for better or ill — that royalty was distant enough to take little interest in our experimentations unless they provided direct benefit to themselves, whereas the Separatists were interested in knowledge and were desperate to explore all scientific options available to them to turn the tide. However, their frail sensibilities would not so easily accept my experimentations.

Ah, to be left to one's own devices or to be famously scrutinized, reviled, and revered in equal measure! The decision weighed upon me so heavily it gave me mild indigestion during my evening banquets. What direction should I choose to advance my most important scientific work?
Down with the Monarchy

The length and difficulty of my journey was exacerbated by the ongoing conflict. Compounding this harried inconvenience, my spouse and I suffered the indignity of a lengthy interrogation by soldiers of the Separatist forces, who had imposed an unofficial martial government.

Peasants-turned-soldiers in their motley uniforms keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost waving a sanguine flag. They spoke of freedom as they dug fresh graves in the cemetery - the wrought iron gates perpetually wreathed in lilies. I observed the daily horse-drawn carts, dragging the wounded towards ill-equipped infirmaries - my crimson reflection in the muddy ruts of unpaved highways.

It was both in spite of and because of this brashness that I found myself drawn to the scrappy Separatist upstarts and their eagerness to fight for the capricious whims of the great unwashed. The Separatists were desperate for the advantages that my family's experimentations provided, and while hesitant over our methods, were willing to further our knowledge in return. Unfortunately, this relationship made them more entitled to levy accusations towards us.

However, the influence of the throne was still absolute. If one could ingratiate themselves with the distracted Monarchy, their influence and money was on offer. The peasantry would be too discontent to focus on our more "ambitious" works. Unfortunately, unless experimentation directly benefited them, the Monarchy had no use for it.

Ah, to be left to one's own devices or to be famously scrutinized, reviled, and revered in equal measure! The decision weighed upon me so heavily that I could scarcely enjoy my afternoon pastries. Neither could the muffled wailing coming from the cellar laboratory nor the distant clattering of gunfire at night calm my weary mind. What direction should I choose to advance my most important scientific work?
Seeds of Conflict

Before my spouse and I had even settled our affairs, I was rewarded not only for my family's numerous contributions to the region, but also for the political allegiance I held (or dreadfully inherited as the case may be). Further promises of considerable clout were made if I were to continue to support the war.

As the conflict raged on, it was clear that with my business acumen, noble influence, and burgeoning scientific genius, I would be a highly sought after ally.

I was quick to suggest a few "enhancements" to their battery and presented several advanced weaponry schematics which could prove instrumental to victory.

While the rumors of my parent's eccentricities made them hesitant, the promise of support from my lucrative estate proved too much to resist. If I could demonstrate to them the visceral efficacy of my proposal, they promised further investment. An easy task.
